cues.text: This is MIT 8105, Network Architecture and Protocols.
Study Session 3 covers wireless networking, network security principles and protocols.
We begin with the first chapter, wireless communication.
A wireless network uses electromagnetic waves to carry data, rather than cables.
Let us start with the parts of a wireless local area network, or WLAN.
First there is the access point, or AP, which is the device that stations connect to.
The stations are the client devices, such as laptops and phones.
Next come the antennas, which radiate and receive the signals.
Where one is used, there is also a wireless controller, which manages several access points together.
Behind these sits the distribution network, the wired side that links the access points to the rest of the network.
Finally there are security and authentication services, which decide who may join.
Two names are easy to confuse.
The SSID names a WLAN.
It is the network name you see in the list on your phone.
The BSSID identifies a basic service set, and it is typically the MAC address of an access point's radio or interface.
So the SSID is the human-friendly name of the network, and the BSSID identifies one particular access point radio.
There are three arrangements to know.
Infrastructure mode uses access points, and clients talk through them.
Ad hoc mode connects peers directly to each other, with no access point.
Mesh uses cooperating nodes that relay traffic for one another, together with backhaul links between them.
Wi-Fi uses shared spectrum, so only one device can usefully transmit at a time on a channel.
It generally uses CSMA/CA, which is carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance.
The sequence is this.
A station listens first, then waits a random backoff, then transmits, and the receiver sends an acknowledgement.
This differs from legacy Ethernet, which used CSMA/CD, carrier sense multiple access with collision detection.
Two problems reduce performance.
One is the hidden node: two stations can both reach the access point but cannot hear each other, so they may transmit at the same time.
The other is interference.
RTS/CTS, which stands for request to send and clear to send, can help in some hidden-node situations.
Now the standards table.
It has three columns: the standard, its typical band, and its key feature together with its headline theoretical maximum.
We take the rows in order.
First, 802.11a.
It works in the 5 GHz band, uses OFDM, which is orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing, and has a headline maximum of 54 megabits per second.
Second, 802.11b.
It works in the 2.4 GHz band and uses DSSS/CCK, direct-sequence spread spectrum with complementary code keying.
Its maximum is 11 megabits per second.
Third, 802.11g.
It also works in 2.4 GHz and uses OFDM, with a maximum of 54 megabits per second.
So it brings the speed of 802.11a to the 2.4 GHz band.
Fourth, 802.11n, also called Wi-Fi 4.
It works in 2.4 and 5 GHz.
Its key feature is MIMO, multiple input multiple output, which uses several antennas, and it reaches up to 600 megabits per second.
Fifth, 802.11ac, also called Wi-Fi 5.
It works in 5 GHz.
Its features are wider channels and MU-MIMO, multi-user MIMO, and it reaches multi-gigabit rates.
Sixth, 802.11ax, called Wi-Fi 6, or Wi-Fi 6E.
It works in 2.4 and 5 GHz, and in 6 GHz for 6E.
Its key feature is OFDMA, orthogonal frequency-division multiple access, which gives better efficiency, and it reaches up to 9.6 gigabits per second.
Note that these headline rates are ideal aggregate physical-layer values.
They are not guaranteed user throughput.
Wi-Fi 7, or 802.11be, is supplementary to this table.
It adds features including multi-link operation, and wider channels where they are permitted.
Now some trade-offs.
The 2.4 GHz band generally offers longer reach, but it is congested.
The 5 and 6 GHz bands offer more spectrum, but with propagation and regulatory trade-offs.
In many regulatory domains, channels 1, 6 and 11 are the common non-overlapping 20 MHz channels in 2.4 GHz.
You should confirm the rules for your own country.
Several factors affect capacity: channel width, interference, signal strength, SNR (signal-to-noise ratio), obstacles, airtime, and client capability.
The practical lesson is that a site survey, careful AP placement and good wired backhaul matter more than simply adding transmit power.
Finally, consider how you would configure an access point.
This is to be done in an isolated lab.
You would take these steps: Select an authorised SSID.
Choose the band, channel and width.
Secure management access.
Use WPA2 or WPA3-Enterprise where supported.
Use RADIUS authentication, with an appropriate VLAN.
Set up a separate guest network with client isolation.
Configure DHCP and firewall policy.
Afterwards you verify association, roaming, coverage, throughput and isolation.
Avoid default passwords, and avoid unauthorised monitoring.
